title: How to Choose a Partner Portal Builder You Can Safely Hand to Subcontractors
summary: Give subcontractors and outside specialists their own login, show each only their jobs, and remove access in one step.
body_markdown:
A solar installer works with six subcontracted install crews. For every job, each crew needs three things: the address, the panel layout, and whether the permit has cleared. Right now they get all of it from a shared Google Drive folder.


That folder also holds every homeowner's signed contract and the sheet showing the company's margin on each job. Nobody chose to share the margins. Someone shared the parent folder two years ago, and nobody has checked it since.


That's usually when growing service businesses start looking for a partner portal builder. The crews haven't complained. The person who signs off on access has just realized they can't say who can see what.


## TL;DR


- A partner portal gives subcontractors, outside specialists, and referral firms their own login. Each one sees only the jobs, files, and tasks they're working on.
- In this article, "partner" means people who do part of the work with you. It doesn't mean resellers or affiliates, which need a different kind of software (PRM).
- Third parties were involved in 48% of confirmed breaches in Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, up from 30% the year before. That puts partner access on the desk of whoever signs off on risk, not just the ops team.
- Five things to test before you pick a tool: each partner sees only their own records, you can hide specific fields, you can remove someone in one step, you can see who changed what, and automations follow the same access rules as people.
- An AI portal builder can build the portal from a description. Check that the access rules come with the build, not as something you add and test yourself afterward.


## What is a partner portal builder, and what does "partner" mean here?


A partner portal builder is software for creating a secure website where people outside your company log in, see the work they're part of, and do their share of it. They might accept a job, upload a site photo, or mark a task done. You decide what each person can see and change.


"Partner" covers two very different groups, and each needs different software:


- **Delivery partners** do part of the work with you: a subcontracted install crew, an outside tax specialist an accounting firm brings in for one client, a freight carrier, or a law firm that refers a case and stays involved. They need job details, files, and tasks.
- **Channel partners** sell for you. Resellers and affiliates need deal registration, commission tracking, and sales material. Tools built for this are usually called partner relationship management (PRM) software.


This article is about delivery partners. If you're running a reseller program, PRM software is the better place to start.


Two more terms often get mixed up. An **AI app builder** creates any kind of app from a prompt. It's fast, and often a good fit for a prototype or an internal tool with one type of user. An **AI portal builder** uses AI to build a portal where several types of people (your team, clients, and partners) work in the same system with different access, and where access rules and workflows are part of the build. Our glossary has a longer explanation of[what an AI portal builder is](https://noloco.io/glossary/ai-portal-builder) .


## Why does partner access become a risk as a service business grows?


With three subcontractors, the owner knows who has access to what. With twenty, spread across different jobs and clients, nobody really does. Access gets added when a job starts and rarely gets removed when it ends.


The wider numbers point the same way. Third parties were involved in 48% of confirmed breaches in[Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report](https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/T167/reports/2026-dbir-data-breach-investigations-report.pdf) , up from 30% in the 2025 edition. In a 2025 study of 1,942 IT and security practitioners by the Ponemon Institute for[Imprivata](https://www.imprivata.com/sites/imprivata/files/2025-02/eBook_Imprivata%20Ponemon%20Report_third-party%20access%20risk_FINAL.pdf) , 47% of organizations said they'd had a breach or cyberattack involving third-party access in the past 12 months. In the same study, 44% said managing third-party permissions was overwhelming for their teams.


Both studies include large companies. For a 50-person service business, the risk is smaller and more ordinary: a subcontractor who can still open the job folder six months after the job ended, or an outside specialist who can see every client's file because there was no simple way to share just one.


**Key takeaways**


- Partner access usually grows one job at a time and is rarely removed when the job ends.
- Third parties were involved in 48% of confirmed breaches in Verizon's 2026 report.
- A useful test for whoever signs off: can you list who has access to what today, in under ten minutes?


## What are the main ways to give partners access, and how do they compare?


Most service businesses end up choosing between four options: shared folders and email, PRM software, a general AI app builder, or an AI portal builder. The table compares them on the questions a sign-off person usually asks.


What you're checking Shared folders and email Partner relationship (PRM) software General AI app builder AI portal builder


**Built for** Sharing files quickly Reseller and affiliate programs Any app from a prompt Portals used by your team, clients, and partners


**Each partner sees only their own jobs** ⚠️ Only if you set up a folder per partner and keep it current ⚠️ For deals and leads, not delivery work ⚠️ Depends on how the app was built ✅ Set once as a rule on the data


**Hide specific fields, like margins** ❌ No, whole files are shared ⚠️ Varies by tool ⚠️ Usually needs custom work ✅ Usually supported, check per tool


**Remove a partner in one step** ❌ Access sits in many folders and threads ✅ Yes ⚠️ Depends on the build ✅ Yes


**Log of who changed what** ⚠️ File activity only ✅ Usually ⚠️ Often not included ✅ Usually, check per tool


**Partners do tasks, not just view files** ❌ No ⚠️ Sales tasks only ✅ If you build them ✅ Forms, approvals, status updates


**Works with data you already have** ✅ Yes ❌ Usually a separate system ⚠️ Often starts with a new database ✅ Connects to Airtable, Google Sheets, or a database


**Best fit** A handful of partners and low-risk files Selling through partners Prototypes and tools for one type of user Many partners on many jobs, with clients involved too


Shared folders work fine for a handful of partners and low-risk files. The trouble starts when the same folder has to serve many partners on many jobs, and when clients need access too. At that point, access has to follow rules on the data, not depend on someone remembering to set up a folder for each job.


**Key takeaways**


- PRM software is built for selling through partners, not for subcontractors doing the work.
- With shared folders, you share whole files, so you can't hide a margin or another client's name inside one.
- With general AI app builders, the access rules depend on how the app was built, so you'll need to test them yourself.


## What should a partner see, and what should they never see?


Before comparing tools, write down what each type of partner needs to see and what they should never see. This list becomes the test you run on every tool. A few examples from different businesses:


- **Solar installer, subcontracted install crew.** Sees: job address, panel layout, permit status, the site photos they uploaded. Never sees: contract value, margins, other crews' jobs.
- **Accounting firm, outside tax specialist.** Sees: the one client file they were brought in for, the filing deadline, the documents requested. Never sees: other clients, fee agreements.
- **Logistics company, freight carrier.** Sees: loads assigned to them, pickup windows, a place to upload proof of delivery. Never sees: rates paid to other carriers, the customer list.
- **Consultancy, outside specialist.** Sees: tasks assigned to them, the deliverables they're working on. Never sees: the project budget, other specialists' day rates.


A good partner portal builder lets you turn each line into a rule once, for example "crews see jobs assigned to their company." That rule then applies to every new job automatically. If someone has to set access by hand each time a job starts, you'll end up back where the shared folder left you.


If most of your partners are field contractors, our guide to[what to look for in a contractor management portal](https://noloco.io/blog/7-things-to-look-for-in-a-contractor-management-portal) goes deeper into compliance documents, change orders, and payment status.


## What questions should you ask before you pick a partner portal builder?


Take these questions into every demo or trial. The middle column shows what a good answer sounds like, and the last column shows when to be careful.


Question to ask What a good answer looks like Be careful if


**Can each partner see only the records linked to them?** Access is set by a rule, like "crews see jobs assigned to their company," and applies to new jobs automatically Access is set by hand for each page or folder


**Can I hide specific fields, not just whole records?** A partner sees the job but not its margin or contract value It's all or nothing for each record


**How fast can I remove a partner?** One action removes their login and closes every link they saved You have to find and remove them in several places


**Can I see who viewed or changed what?** A log shows each change and who made it, including external users There's no log, or it only covers your own team


**Do automations and AI follow the same access rules?** Automations and any AI assistant only touch the records their role allows Automations run with full access by default


**Can partners, clients, and my team work in the same system?** One system, with a different view for each role Each group needs its own tool, with data copied between them


**Does it work with the data we already have?** It connects to your current spreadsheet, Airtable base, or database You have to move everything over before you can start


**How does pricing change as we add partners?** Limits for external users are published on the pricing page Every new subcontractor becomes a new seat to approve


**Can partners log in on our own domain?** Yes, for example portal.yourcompany.com Partners only ever see the vendor's web address


Two questions catch most problems early. Ask how access is set for a brand new job, and ask what happens to a partner's saved links after you remove them. If the vendor can't answer both clearly, keep looking.


**Key takeaways**


- Access should follow rules on the data, not be set by hand per page or folder.
- Removing a partner should take one action and close every link they saved.
- Automations and AI assistants need the same limits as the people using the portal.


## How do you test a partner portal builder before partners log in?


A demo shows you the tool working with sample data. Before partners log in, you need to know it works with your real data and your real rules. Plan for about two hours per tool.


**Before you start, have ready:**


- A copy of the data from one recent, finished job
- Your "sees / never sees" list from the section above
- Two test email addresses, one for a test partner and one for a test client


**Steps:**


1. Connect the copy of your real job data instead of using the vendor's sample data.
2. Create a partner role from your "sees / never sees" list.
3. Log in as the test partner and try to open a job that isn't theirs, by searching for it and by editing the link in the address bar.
4. Check that hidden fields, like margin, don't show up in exports, search results, or email notifications.
5. As the test partner, complete one real task, such as uploading a site photo, and check who gets notified.
6. Remove the test partner, then try to log in and open a link they saved.
7. Open the change log and confirm the upload and the removal both appear.


**Example:** a solar installer loads one finished job, creates an "install crew" role, and logs in as a test crew. The crew can see the job address and panel layout. Then the installer tries changing the job number in the link to another customer's job. If that job opens, the tool fails the test, however good the demo looked.


## Where does an AI portal builder fit, and where does an AI app builder fit?


Both can save weeks of work. The difference is between building something quickly and running real work on it with people outside your company.


**Use an AI app builder when:**


- Only your own team will use it, at least for now
- You're testing an idea and expect to rebuild it
- The app doesn't need to connect to data you already keep elsewhere


**Choose an AI portal builder when:**


- Partners and clients need their own login
- Each person must see only their own jobs, files, and tasks
- The portal has to work with data you already have, such as a spreadsheet or Airtable base
- You'll keep changing it as you add partners, job types, and steps


**Can an AI app builder handle partner logins?** Yes, but you usually have to design the access rules yourself and test them again every time the app changes.


**Do you need a developer to set up an AI portal builder?** Usually not for the setup. Plan time for someone in operations to write the access rules and run the tests above.


**Can you start with an AI app builder and switch later?** Yes. Expect to rebuild the access rules and logins when you do, and to retest them before partners log in again.

## Final thoughts


The right partner portal builder for a growing service business isn't the one with the longest feature list. It's the one where you can say, in under ten minutes, exactly what each subcontractor and outside specialist can see, and remove any of them in one step.


Start with your "sees / never sees" list, take the questions above into every demo, and test with a real job before any partner logs in. If most of your partners work in the field, use our[contractor management portal checklist](https://noloco.io/blog/7-things-to-look-for-in-a-contractor-management-portal) as your next step.


## Frequently asked questions


**What is the difference between a partner portal and a client portal?**
A client portal is for the people you deliver work to. A partner portal is for the people who help you deliver it, like subcontractors or outside specialists. Many service businesses need both, and it's often simpler to run them in one system where each group has its own view.


**Should each subcontractor have their own login, or can a company share one?**
Give each person their own login. Shared logins make it impossible to see who changed what, and you can't remove one person without cutting off everyone else at that company.


**Is a shared Google Drive or Dropbox folder enough for partner access?**
For a few partners and low-risk files, often yes. It stops being enough when you need to hide part of a file, when partners need to do tasks rather than just download files, or when you can't easily check who still has access.


**How do you remove a subcontractor's access when a job ends?**
In a portal, you remove their role or their access to that job, and they lose access to everything linked to it. With shared folders, you have to find and remove them from each folder, thread, and file link separately, which is where access gets missed.


**What is the difference between partner portal software and PRM software?**
PRM (partner relationship management) software is built for channel partners who sell for you, with deal registration and commission tracking. A partner portal for delivery partners is built around jobs, files, tasks, and approvals.


**Can AI tools or automations safely use partner data?**
Yes, if they follow the same access rules as people. An automation or AI assistant should only read and change the records its role allows, and its actions should show up in the same log as everyone else's.
